cur:objects-monza-ampulla-adoration.summary: The face of this pilgrim's flask shows the Virgin enthroned frontally with the Christ Child on her lap, with the star above; the Magi approach from one side bearing gifts and the shepherds with their flocks from the other. A Greek inscription runs around the rim. Brought back from the Holy Land filled with oil from the holy places, such flasks carried images of the Gospel events that had taken place there.
facts: Wikipedia describes the Monza ampullae as the largest collection of Early Medieval pilgrimage flasks for holy oil from the Holy Land, made in Palestine probably in the 5th to early 7th centuries and kept in Monza Cathedral since they were donated by Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards (c. 570–628).
They were mass-produced souvenirs, filled with oil from lamps burning before the holy shrines, and their images played a crucial part in establishing the iconography of many Christian subjects.
cur:objects-monza-ampulla-adoration.notes: The only freely licensed image found is a historic glass lantern slide (University of Leuven) reproducing an engraving of the ampulla, not a photograph of the object. The specific ampulla number in Monza could not be identified.

met:460946.summary: In this gilt-bronze pax, the Virgin sits enthroned before a backdrop of classical arches and buildings, tenderly drawing the Christ Child to her cheek while the young Saint John the Baptist, haloed, leans against her knee. Her mantle falls in rich patterned folds, and the whole is enclosed in an elaborate scrolled frame with cherub heads. A pax was offered to the faithful to kiss during Mass as the sign of peace, so this intimate image of the Holy Family was made to be touched in devotion.
facts: The Met dates the model to the third quarter and this cast to the last quarter of the 16th century, probably Rome.
The frame was cast in four separate parts and riveted at each corner; the reverse has a reddish-brown patina while the face is gilt.
It belongs to the Robert Lehman Collection, given to the Met in 1975.
met:460946.notes: Worklist year 900 was an error: this is a late Renaissance work (late 16th century). It depicts the Christ Child, so it remains in the collection, but belongs with 16th-century works.
